protocol.instrument_name: Management for Overweight and Obesity – Clinical Practice Guideline
protocol.legal_basis: Authorisation page (p2): 'Community Pharmacy Expanded Scope of Practice Initiative. In accordance with regulation 17A of the Controlled Substances (Poisons) Regulations 2011 (the Poisons Regulations) a pharmacist is authorised to prescribe a prescription drug (not being a drug of dependence) if the pharmacist is included on the register of authorised pharmacists and the drug is prescribed in accordance with the Community Pharmacist Prescribing Code.'
protocol.supervision_model: Document does not use 'collaborative'/'autonomous' terminology; its own wording: an authorised pharmacist on the register of authorised pharmacists prescribing in accordance with the Community Pharmacist Prescribing Code (p2). Service restriction (p3): 'Service restricted to patients aged 18 years or over.' Discretion clause (p6): 'When applying the information contained within this clinical practice guideline, pharmacists are advised to exercise professional discretion and judgement. The clinical practice guideline does not override the responsibility of the pharmacist to make decisions appropriate to the circumstances of the individual, in consultation with the patient and/or their carer.' Multidisciplinary expectation (p6): 'Effective and long-term management of overweight and obesity requires a multidisciplinary team care approach ... including pharmacists, medical practitioners, dietitians, exercise physiologists and psychologists (11, 21-23).' Confirm-management requirement (p11): 'Pharmacists must consult the Therapeutic Guidelines, Australian Medicines Handbook and other relevant references to confirm the treatment recommendation is appropriate, including for: contraindications and precautions; drug interactions.'
protocol.scope_summary: SA Health (Community Pharmacy Expanded Scope of Practice Initiative) clinical practice guideline for pharmacist management of overweight and obesity in adults. Service restricted to patients aged 18 years or over. Covers: 'Refer when' conditions requiring referral to a general practitioner (pregnancy/breastfeeding, BMI > 40 kg/m2, specialist-managed comorbidities, eating disorders, neurodiversity with eating-disorder history, previous bariatric surgery); 'Treat (if clinically appropriate) and concurrently refer' situations (psychiatric disorders, neurodiversity without eating-disorder history, OSA, nutritional deficiencies, active medical weight-reduction treatment, CVD/asthma/COPD, Plan B non-response); key points (BMI ≥ 25 definition, lifestyle modification foundation, multidisciplinary care, person-centred non-judgmental communication); patient history; examination and screening; investigation (Table 2: HbA1c/FBG, serum lipids, BP with testing and referral thresholds including immediate/emergency thresholds); Management Plan A (initial weight-loss strategies: 5As counselling, RED/LED diets, dietitian referral) and Management Plan B (secondary strategies: VLEDs, pharmacotherapy — Orlistat with printed eligibility criteria, liver function monitoring); goal setting (5-10% weight loss); confirm management; communicate plan; monthly clinical review; Appendix 1 co-morbidity screening (STOP-BANG, BMI/waist, K10, SCOFF, AUSDRISK, dyslipidaemia signs); Appendix 2 Weight Management Plan template; Appendix 3 references. 'Ineligibility for treatment as part of a prescribing service does not preclude a patient from accessing services provided as part of usual pharmacy care.'

inclusion.text: 'Service restricted to patients aged 18 years or over.'

'Each patient's needs regarding weight management and suitability for pharmacist management should be assessed on a case-by-case basis. Sufficient information should be obtained from the patient to assess the safety and appropriateness of any recommendations and medicines.'

inclusion.text: 'The patient history should consider:' age; 'pregnancy and breastfeeding status (if applicable)'; 'history of eating disorders (or disordered eating) – perform SCOFF questionnaire at this stage (prior to discussion regarding weight history) if there is any concern regarding disordered eating'; 'weight history including highest and lowest weights (and when)'; 'previous weight loss and strategies used (including the degree of success and levels of medical/health practitioner support (e.g., previous drug therapy, very-low calorie diets (VLCD), exercise)'; 'recent relevant biochemical markers (see Investigations)'; 'medical conditions and comorbidities, including weight and non-weight related'; 'history of neurodiversity'; 'surgical history, including any bariatric surgery'; 'current medication (including prescribed medicines, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, herbs, powders (e.g., protein powders), other supplements)'; 'drug allergies/adverse drug effects'; 'alcohol and drug history'; 'smoking status'; 'diet history (usual intake over the last 6-month period) and fluid intake'; 'current level of physical activity (structured and incidental activity)'; 'other factors impacting upon successful weight management: cooking/shopping skills; health and nutritional literacy; cooking/shopping responsibilities, including the number of people in the household; stage of readiness to change; patient support networks.'

'All patients should undergo basic screening and an examination for common weight-related comorbidities. Information to guide screening has been provided in Appendix 1. However, it is also recommended that the patient be referred to their usual medical practitioner to be comprehensively screened.'

'Recommended investigations are outlined in Table 2. If available, recent test results may be used (e.g., provided by a medical practitioner with referral or available on My Health Record) if there have been no changes to the patient's medication or health status and the test was conducted within the past 12 months.'

The presentation is within the Service's clinical focus — 'Excess weight (overweight and obesity), generally defined as a body mass index (BMI) ≥ 25, is a risk factor for metabolic and chronic conditions, including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease (CVD) and some cancers, leading to higher rates of premature morbidity and mortality (11, 12).'

No 'Refer when' condition is present at presentation (EXC-1 to EXC-6), or the situation is managed under a 'Treat (if clinically appropriate) and concurrently refer' exception (EXC-7 to EXC-12 / EXE-2 to EXE-7). Management is 'in accordance with the Australian Obesity Management Algorithm ... centred around lifestyle interventions (initial weight-loss strategies) that are tailored to relevant factors for the individual.'

exclusion.text: Refer when — 'Referral to a general practitioner (or other medical practitioner where appropriate) is required if: The patient is pregnant or breastfeeding.'
Refer when: The patient has a BMI > 40 kg/m2.

Refer when: The patient has a comorbidity that requires specialist medical management for weight loss, including (but not limited to): Chronic kidney disease; Hepatic impairment or liver disease; Thyroid and endocrine disorders, including diabetes when being treated with insulin or sulfonylureas (as they are associated with weight gain); Anaemia; Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS); Gastrointestinal disorders including coeliac disease, Crohn's disease, gastroparesis, peptic ulcer; Epilepsy or history of seizures; Idiopathic intracranial hypertension; Patients taking a medicine associated with weight gain; Patients taking warfarin. [list printed as 'including (but not limited to)' — non-exhaustive]
Refer when: The patient has an eating disorder (e.g., binge eating, anorexia nervosa, bulimia), or a history of eating disorders.
Refer when: The patient has a diagnosed history of neurodiversity (e.g., ADHD) with a history of an eating disorder.
Refer when: The patient has previously undergone bariatric surgery.

Treat (if clinically appropriate) and concurrently refer — 'Provide initial treatment and concurrently refer to a general practitioner (or other medical practitioner where approriate) for collaborative management in the following situations: Patients with diagnosed (or suspected) psychiatric disorders, including psychosis, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depression, anxiety.' [source prints 'approriate']

steps.description: Examination and screening — 'All patients should undergo basic screening and an examination for common weight-related comorbidities. Information to guide screening has been provided in Appendix 1. However, it is also recommended that the patient be referred to their usual medical practitioner to be comprehensively screened.' Measurements: 'Measurement of BMI and waist circumference at commencement and regular reviews (recommended monthly)' (p15). 'NB1: Body Mass Index (BMI) is a screening tool only and may not be the most clinically appropriate assessment for all patients (e.g., consider also using waist circumference, waist to hip ratio, body fat percentage and skin fold measurements) (2).' Waist cutoffs (p15-16): 'Males with a waist circumference ≥ 94 cm are at increased risk of CVD and other comorbidities (≥ 102cm = a greatly increased risk, especially if BMI > 25)'; 'Females with a waist circumference ≥ 80 cm are at increased risk (≥ 88cm = a greatly increased risk, especially if BMI >25).'

steps.description: Investigation — 'Recommended investigations are outlined in Table 2. If available, recent test results may be used (e.g., provided by a medical practitioner with referral or available on My Health Record) if there have been no changes to the patient's medication or health status and the test was conducted within the past 12 months.' Table 2 rows as printed: 'HbA1c or Fasting blood glucose (FBG) — Testing requirements: People without previous diagnosis of diabetes: HbA1c ≥ 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) OR Fasting blood glucose ≥ 7.0 mmol/L AND at least one of the criteria (refer to testing requirements for people without diabetes) AND no HbA1c or FBG test results from previous 3 years → Concurrent referral to medical practitioner for further investigation of diabetes.' 'Immediate/emergency referral: A HbA1c > 10% (86mmol/mol) or any blood glucose level ≥ 20.0 mmol/L is indicative of severe hyperglycaemia and is a medical emergency in patients who are unwell (e.g., there are signs of ketosis, dehydration, vomiting, signs or symptoms of underlying infection, confusion and/or delirium/altered level of consciousness) (32).' 'Serum lipids — Testing requirements: If lipid testing has not been performed in the previous 5 years AND one or more of the criteria [ATSI ≥35; non-ATSI ≥45; one or more classical signs or symptoms of diabetes (weight loss, polyuria, polydipsia, blurred vision)] → Concurrent referral ... if one or more of the following test result thresholds are met: TC ≥ 5.5 mmol/L (or < 4.0 mmol/L for people on lipid modifying drug therapy); LDL-C ≥ 2.0 mmol/L; HDL-C ≤ 1.0mmol; Triglycerides ≥ 2.0 mmol/L.' 'Blood pressure (BP) — Testing requirements: All patients → Concurrent referral if BP ≥ 140/90 mmHg. Immediate/ emergency referral: Systolic BP ≥ 180 and/or diastolic BP ≥ 110 mmHg is considered to be severe hypertension and is a medical emergency in patients with signs or symptoms of a hypertensive urgency (headache or dizziness).' Risk-criteria list for testing (people without previous diagnosis of diabetes): 'AUSDRISK score ≥ 12; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples; Pacific Islander/Indian sub-continent/Southern European/Asian background; History of gestational diabetes; Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS); Taking antipsychotic medicines; Aged >40 and overweight or obese; Impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) or impaired fasting glucose (IFG) previously recorded; First degree relative with diabetes; One or more classical signs or symptoms of diabetes.' 'NB1: Limitations of HbA1c: HbA1c tests may be inaccurate in the presence of certain conditions (e.g., haemoglobinopathies, haemolytic anaemia, sickle cell anaemia, pregnancy, chronic renal failure, liver disease, macrocytosis, alcoholism, iron deficiency).'

Obstructive Sleep Apnoea: 'Requirements: All patients: Inquiry into possible sleep apnoea and associated symptoms prior to consideration of management (e.g., snoring, daytime somnolence, fatigue, lack of energy, reduced concentration)'; 'Screening tests: ... STOP-Bang Questionnaire'; 'Concurrent referral to a medical practitioner for further investigation is recommended for all patients suspected of having sleep apnoea or another weight-related respiratory condition, for example: Patients with at least one risk factor or comorbidity + multiple symptoms of sleep apnoea; A score of ≥ 3 on the STOP-Bang Questionnaire.' BMI and waist circumference: 'Referral to a medical practitioner or specialist weight loss service is recommended for people with: BMI > 40 kg/m2'. Mental health/psychological distress: 'Concurrent referral to a medical practitioner is recommended for patients suspected of having a mental health disorder or in psychological distress, for example: Patients who score ≥ 20 on the K10.' Eating disorders: 'Referral to a medical practitioner is recommended for patients who score ≥ 2 on the SCOFF questionnaire. Pharmacists may commence management and concurrently refer to a medical practitioner for patients who score < 2 on the SCOFF questionnaire.' Diabetes: 'A risk assessment tool (e.g., Australian Type 2 Diabetes Risk Assessment Tool (AUSDRISK)) can be used ... Patients aged > 40 years: Risk of developing type 2 diabetes should be estimated every 3 years using AUSDRISK. For patients with clinical signs of insulin resistance (e.g., weight gain, fatigue, acanthosis nigricans): Fasting blood glucose and/or HbA1c test required, even if no symptoms are present.' Dyslipidaemia: 'Concurrent referral to a medical practitioner is recommended for patients with a history of familial hypercholesterolemia. Consider screening for: Clinical signs (family history) of familial hypercholesterolemia (e.g., tendon xanthomata, arcus cornealis prior to age 45, xanthelasma).'

steps.description: Management and treatment plan — 'The management of overweight and obesity, in accordance with the Australian Obesity Management Algorithm, is centred around lifestyle interventions (initial weight-loss strategies) that are tailored to relevant factors for the individual. All management plans should include recommendations regarding lifestyle modification. Lifestyle modification refers to achieving positive changes in diet, physical activity and/or behaviour (11).' 'Pharmacist management of overweight and obesity may involve: Lifestyle modification strategies such as brief advice; Referral to a dietitian for specialised and individualised advice; Providing education and counselling on weight management medicines (for example Orlistat).' Management Plan A (Initial weight-loss strategies): brief advice via the '5As counselling' structure (Assess, Advise, Agree, Assist, Arrange); 'calorie intake can be reduced by approximately 500kcal/day using Australian Guide to Healthy Eating resources (AGHE)' with 'combined restrictive eating plans that adhere to Australian Dietary Guideline (ADG) recommendations ... referred to as low calorie diets (LCDs)'; 'Involvement of other healthcare professionals, particularly for support and maintenance strategies.' Management Plan B (Secondary weight loss strategies): 'calorie intake can be reduced to between 800 to 1200 kcal/day using established commercially available very-low calorie diets (VLCDs)'; 'Require nutritional supervision by a dietitian for the duration of the diet (21, 23). There are major concerns about long-term use and also about insufficient provision of vitamins, minerals and trace elements. Weigh loss achieved must be maintained by a sensible eating plan incorporating behavioural strategies (28, 31).' Pharmacotherapy: 'For patients following Management Plan A showing less than a 5% decrease in weight after 3 months AND with a BMI > 27 (if other CVD risk factors present) or a BMI > 30 (no other CVD risk factors or comorbidities): prescribe Orlistat in accordance with the Australian Medicines Handbook: Orlistat (4, 36). The liver function of patients prescribed Orlistat should be monitored (4).' 'If Orlistat is unsuitable, refer to a medical practitioner for other pharmacological management.' NB3: 'Orlistat is Schedule 3 medicine that may be considered as part of standard pharmacist care. Please refer to the Pharmaceutical Society of Australia's Guidance for provision of Pharmacist Only medicine (Orlistat) within a professional pharmacy service framework. In addition, pharmacists may wish to complete the General risk minimisation measures for Orlistat (10).' Goals: 'Patients can achieve 5-10% weight loss in the first 6-months of management with Management Plan A; Patients can achieve up to 10% weight loss in the first 6-months of Management Plan B; Patients can achieve a 5-10% weight loss at the 12-months of management.' 'Pharmacists must consult the Therapeutic Guidelines, Australian Medicines Handbook and other relevant references to confirm the treatment recommendation is appropriate, including for: contraindications and precautions; drug interactions.'

steps.description: Communicate agreed management plan — 'The agreed management plan should be discussed with the patient. The agreed management plan should be reiterate with each member of the patient's care team, with the patient's consent (25). Verbal and written information, such as handouts and worksheets, may assist with counselling, particularly for complex information that may be difficult to remember (e.g., directions on how to use a product) (25).' Counselling items (p11): 'how to use; dosage regimen and administration (if applicable); expected benefits of the medicine; how to manage adverse effects, including serious adverse effects requiring medical care; when to seek further care and/or.' Applicable to medication counselling, monitoring, administration, storage and disposal (p11). Lifestyle modification brief advice (5As) and tailored eating/physical-activity guidance; 'Relevant resources to support with the agreed management plan (p12): Better Health Coaching Service; Preventive Health SA – Eating well; Baker Heart and Diabetes Institute Health Hub factsheets; Australian Government Eat for health calculators; The Obesity Collective; Weight Issues Network | Weight Stigma in Australia; National Association of Clinical Obesity Services.' The written Weight Management Plan (Appendix 2) captures the agreed plan, monitoring plan, targets and supports.

steps.description: Clinical review — 'Arranging a follow up and clinical review with the patient is an important component of overweight and obesity management. Clinical review with the pharmacist should occur in line with recommendations in the Australian Obesity Management Algorithm and other relevant guidelines. Clinical review on a monthly basis is recommended to monitor progress towards the weight loss target, efficacy of lifestyle modification, and to monitor for adverse effects. Clinical review appointments should include: weight and waist circumference measurements, and BMI calculation; blood pressure monitoring; brief advice and reinforcement of lifestyle modification; questioning relating to any new onset eating behaviours that may suggest an eating disorder; review of adverse effects. Pharmacists may also consider repeating laboratory testing (where indicated). Pharmacists should generally only prescribe a sufficient quantity of medicine (including repeats) for the period until the patient's next review.' Also: 'Weight loss goals should be set in collaboration with the patient and reviewed regularly' (p11); BMI and waist circumference 'at commencement and regular reviews (recommended monthly)' (p15); diabetes risk estimated every 3 years in patients aged > 40 using AUSDRISK (p16).

treatments.notes: Eligibility verbatim (p11): 'For patients following Management Plan A showing less than a 5% decrease in weight after 3 months AND with a BMI > 27 (if other CVD risk factors present) or a BMI > 30 (no other CVD risk factors or comorbidities): prescribe Orlistat in accordance with the Australian Medicines Handbook: Orlistat (4, 36).' Monitoring verbatim (p11): 'The liver function of patients prescribed Orlistat should be monitored (4).' Unsuitability verbatim (p11): 'If Orlistat is unsuitable, refer to a medical practitioner for other pharmacological management.' Supply status verbatim (p11, NB3): 'Orlistat is Schedule 3 medicine that may be considered as part of standard pharmacist care. Please refer to the Pharmaceutical Society of Australia's Guidance for provision of Pharmacist Only medicine (Orlistat) within a professional pharmacy service framework. In addition, pharmacists may wish to complete the General risk minimisation measures for Orlistat (10).' Safety check verbatim (p11): 'Pharmacists must consult the Therapeutic Guidelines, Australian Medicines Handbook and other relevant references to confirm the treatment recommendation is appropriate, including for: contraindications and precautions; drug interactions.' Pregnancy caveat verbatim (p4): 'Referral to a general practitioner (or other medical practitioner where appropriate) is required if: The patient is pregnant or breastfeeding' — pregnancy and breastfeeding are exclusion/referral conditions for this Service (EXC-1 / RF-1). Paediatric/age caveat verbatim (p3): 'Service restricted to patients aged 18 years or over.' No strength, dose, route, frequency, duration or maximum dose is printed anywhere in this document — regimen delegated to 'Australian Medicines Handbook: Orlistat' (refs 4, 36) and PSA Guidance (see open_questions / hugh_to_confirm). Note: the AMH resource list also names Liraglutide, Naltrexone with bupropion, Phentermine, Semaglutide and Tirzepatide (p13) but the Service prescribes only Orlistat — other pharmacological management requires referral (EXC-14). The document's primary management strategies are non-drug lifestyle interventions (Management Plan A/B: 5As counselling, LCDs, VLCDs, dietitian referral) (p9-10).

red_flags.trigger_text: Refer when — 'Referral to a general practitioner (or other medical practitioner where appropriate) is required if: The patient is pregnant or breastfeeding.'
Refer when: The patient has a BMI > 40 kg/m2.

Refer when: The patient has a comorbidity that requires specialist medical management for weight loss, including (but not limited to): Chronic kidney disease; Hepatic impairment or liver disease; Thyroid and endocrine disorders, including diabetes when being treated with insulin or sulfonylureas (as they are associated with weight gain); Anaemia; Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS); Gastrointestinal disorders including coeliac disease, Crohn's disease, gastroparesis, peptic ulcer; Epilepsy or history of seizures; Idiopathic intracranial hypertension; Patients taking a medicine associated with weight gain; Patients taking warfarin. [list printed as 'including (but not limited to)' — non-exhaustive]
Refer when: The patient has an eating disorder (e.g., binge eating, anorexia nervosa, bulimia), or a history of eating disorders.
Refer when: The patient has a diagnosed history of neurodiversity (e.g., ADHD) with a history of an eating disorder.
Refer when: The patient has previously undergone bariatric surgery.

Treat (if clinically appropriate) and concurrently refer: 'Patients with diagnosed (or suspected) psychiatric disorders, including psychosis, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depression, anxiety.'

review_followup.when: Clinical review on a monthly basis
review_followup.what: 'Clinical review on a monthly basis is recommended to monitor progress towards the weight loss target, efficacy of lifestyle modification, and to monitor for adverse effects.'

'Clinical review appointments should include: weight and waist circumference measurements, and BMI calculation; blood pressure monitoring; brief advice and reinforcement of lifestyle modification; questioning relating to any new onset eating behaviours that may suggest an eating disorder; review of adverse effects.'

review_followup.when: At commencement and regular reviews (recommended monthly)
review_followup.what: 'Measurement of BMI and waist circumference at commencement and regular reviews (recommended monthly).'
'Pharmacists may also consider repeating laboratory testing (where indicated).'

review_followup.when: Between reviews — supply limited to the period until the next review
review_followup.what: 'Pharmacists should generally only prescribe a sufficient quantity of medicine (including repeats) for the period until the patient's next review.'

'Weight loss goals should be set in collaboration with the patient and reviewed regularly (38).' Goals: 'Patients can achieve 5-10% weight loss in the first 6-months of management with Management Plan A; Patients can achieve up to 10% weight loss in the first 6-months of Management Plan B; Patients can achieve a 5-10% weight loss at the 12-months of management.'

review_followup.when: Every 3 years for patients aged > 40 years
